title: Grateful Dead Live at Fillmore West on 1968-08-21

ai_review.summary: Soundboard capture of the legendary 8/21/68 gig with a landmark Dark Star, vocal‑led The Eleven and an out‑of‑this‑world Alligator.
ai_review.review: The performance is hailed as one of the best of the magic year ’68 – a powerful second set highlighted by Dark Star → St. Stephen → The Eleven (with vocals) → Death Don't Have No Mercy, plus a scorching Lovelight and an all‑time favorite Alligator.  The soundboard source is generally clear but sounds a bit flatter than other versions, missing some high‑frequency sparkle and the tail of Lovelight, and one reviewer objects to a poorly edited “Drums” track.

ai_rating.rationale: Most reviewers give 4‑5 stars and praise the musical moments; recording issues are noted but not severe, leading to a strong overall rating.

recording_quality.technical_notes: Generally clear soundboard with good organ micding; described as slightly flatter and missing some high‑end detail compared to other versions, Lovelight’s ending is cut off, and one reviewer criticizes a 14‑second “Drums” edit.

show_quality.setlist_flow: The first set is solid with tight playing on Schoolgirl and a mellow Alligator that builds after the brief drum break.  The second set is the show’s centerpiece, delivering the historic Dark Star → St. Stephen → The Eleven sequence and a fiery Lovelight, though the end of Lovelight fades out.

band_member_comments.Jerry: Garcia’s guitar tone is praised as “on fire”; his vocal is low on the Cryptical reprise but shines on Lovelight and Death Don’t Have No Mercy; notable Goodnight theme and interplay with Phil.
band_member_comments.Phil: Lesh’s bass intertwines with Garcia in a “psychic dance” during Dark Star and The Eleven, earning high marks for chemistry.
band_member_comments.Keys: Tom Constanten’s six‑note organ figure in Dark Star is highlighted as memorable; Pigpen’s organ work on Schoolgirl and Alligator receives strong praise, noted as well mic’d.
band_member_comments.Drums: One reviewer objects to a 14‑second “Drums” label that does not reflect the era’s true drum segment.
